# Emergency Fund

## Overview

I built an emergency fund after a winter when the boiler failed and the car needed a clutch in the same month. A reserve holds three months of expenses at a minimum, and I treat that as the floor rather than the target. Once a mortgage, an old boiler and a car are in the picture, six months of expenses is the honest figure, because those three have a habit of failing close together and none of them waits for a good month. The reserve lives in an instant-access savings account at around 3.8%, not in investments, because the point is that the amount is there and known. The whole sum earns a modest rate and that is fine; the job of this money is certainty, not growth. It sits apart from the long-term investing account in every sense, in a different institution with a different login, so that a bad week in the market does not tempt me to raid it and a bad week at home does not force me to sell shares near the bottom. I review the target once a year against actual spending and I raise it when life gets more expensive. The number on the account is the whole point: I know what is in there without opening a portfolio, and I know that no market can shrink it between Tuesday and Friday. That certainty is what the reserve buys, and it is worth the modest rate I give up by keeping the money out of shares.

## Setup

The mechanics are deliberately dull. On payday a standing order sends 400 EUR into the savings account, and I do not look at the balance for the rest of the month. The transfer is automatic because a decision I have to make every month is a decision I will eventually skip. The account is instant access, so the money arrives in my current account within minutes rather than days, which is the only feature that matters here.

The rule is that the reserve is untouched for holidays or a new laptop: those are planned costs, and a planned cost has no business in money meant for a failed boiler. When I do spend from the fund, the rebuilding starts at the next payday and continues until the target is whole again, and I raise the monthly transfer for a few months rather than treating the gap as permanent. I keep the target in a note next to the account, with the monthly figure, the rate and the date I last reviewed it, so a change of circumstances is a two-minute edit rather than a guess.

The account also has a separate card that stays in a drawer, which sounds fussy and has saved the reserve twice. I check the rate twice a year, because 3.8% is not a promise and a better instant-access account is a five-minute switch. When the balance crosses the top of the target I stop the transfer for a month and let the money go to the investment account instead, so the reserve never grows into a second portfolio by accident. I also keep a short list of what counts as an emergency next to the note, since a list written in a calm week is a better judge than I am in a bad one.

## Notes

I keep the emergency fund separate from investing for one reason: they answer different questions. Long-term investing money is meant to be left alone for a decade and to fall in the meantime, and the emergency fund is meant to be available today and never to fall. If the two are mixed, a market drop and a broken boiler arrive as one problem instead of two manageable ones.

I count three to six months of essential spending, not of income, so the number covers rent, food, utilities, insurance and transport, and leaves out holidays and treats. The reserve is also not a replacement for insurance: cover handles the car crash and the medical bill, and the reserve handles the awkward gap and the small disasters an excess does not reach. I keep the target written down and I check it once a year, usually in January when the budget review is already on the desk.

When the reserve is full I send the 400 EUR to the investment account instead, and I stop thinking about it. The rate on the account is not the point; the point is that the money is there on the day I need it, without a sale, a delay or a market at a bad point in its cycle. That is the whole difference between this money and the money I invest. The two accounts do not compete for the same euros, because the reserve is capped at its target and any surplus above it flows to the investment side without a debate.
